domains.description: Timeless programming concepts: data structures, algorithms, complexity, design patterns, idioms. Highest cold-start priority — these are the most frequently asked about during outages.

entries.title: Big-O Notation and Complexity Analysis
entries.claim: Big-O notation describes the asymptotic upper bound of an algorithm's time or space complexity as input size grows.
entries.solution: Big-O: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n), O(n^2) quadratic, O(n^3) cubic, O(2^n) exponential, O(n!) factorial. To analyze: count primitive operations as a function of input size n, drop constants and lower-order terms. Use it to choose data structures/algorithms: prefer O(n log n) sorting over O(n^2) for large n; prefer O(1) hash lookup over O(n) linear search.
assumptions: Input size n is the dominant variable
Primitive operations (comparison, assignment) are O(1)
System has sufficient memory for the chosen approach
invariants: O(1) is always faster than O(n) for large enough n
Lower Big-O wins asymptotically regardless of constant factors
Space-time tradeoff is often available (e.g., hash table uses O(n) space for O(1) lookup
failure_modes: Confusing Big-O (worst-case) with Big-Theta (average-case) with Big-Omega (best-case)
Ignoring cache effects — a cache-friendly O(n^2) can beat a cache-unfriendly O(n log n)
Not considering practical input sizes where constants dominate
counterarguments: Big-O hides constant factors — an O(n) algorithm with a 1000x constant may be slower than O(n^2) for n < 100
Real-world performance depends on hardware, OS scheduling, and cache behavior not captured by Big-O
evidence: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein 'Introduction to Algorithms' — standard reference
Knuth 'The Art of Computer Programming' — formal analysis of algorithmic complexity

entries.title: Hash Tables: Design and Collision Resolution
entries.claim: Hash tables provide average O(1) lookup, insertion, and deletion through a hash function mapping keys to buckets, with collisions resolved via chaining or open addressing.
entries.solution: Hash function h(k) maps key k to bucket index. Collisions: (1) Chaining — each bucket holds a linked list; simple, handles load factor > 1, but uses extra memory for pointers; (2) Open addressing — find next empty slot via linear probing (i+1), quadratic probing (i^2), or double hashing (h2(k)); saves memory but suffers from clustering. Load factor α = n/m; when α > 0.75, resize (rehash) — typically double the bucket array. Good hash functions must be deterministic, uniform, and fast (MurmurHash, FNV-1a, or language builtins).
assumptions: Good hash function distributes keys uniformly
Memory overhead of chaining pointers is acceptable
Hash function computation is O(1)
invariants: Average-case O(1) for all operations at α < 0.75
Worst-case O(n) when all keys collide in one bucket
Resizing (rehash) is O(n) but amortized O(1) per insertion
failure_modes: Hash flooding attack — attacker crafts colliding keys to degrade to O(n)
Poor hash function causes clustering and degraded performance
Forgetting to resize leads to performance degradation
Not using immutable keys causes lookup failures after mutation
counterarguments: For small datasets (< 100 items), linear search in an array may outperform a hash table due to cache locality and no hashing overhead
evidence: Java HashMap uses chaining with tree-bins (red-black tree) for buckets > 8 items
Python dict uses open addressing with pseudo-random probing
Redis uses chaining with incremental rehashing

entries.title: Binary Search and Its Applications
entries.claim: Binary search efficiently finds a target in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search space, achieving O(log n) time and O(1) space (iterative).
entries.solution: Maintain low=0, high=n-1. While low <= high: mid = low + (high-low)//2 (avoid overflow). If arr[mid] == target, return mid. If arr[mid] < target, low = mid+1. Else high = mid-1. Return -1 if not found. Applications: (1) Find in sorted array. (2) Find first/last occurrence (don't return on match, narrow to find boundary). (3) Search in rotated array. (4) Binary search on answer space (e.g., aggressive cows, allocate mail boxes). (5) Binary search on monotonic function.
assumptions: Array is sorted
Random access O(1) — not valid for linked lists
invariants: Each iteration eliminates half the search space
Loop invariant: target is always in [low, high] if it exists
mid computation must avoid integer overflow in languages with fixed-size integers
failure_modes: Off-by-one in loop condition (low < high vs low <= high)
Computing mid as (low+high)//2 overflows in Java/C++
Using binary search on unsorted data gives undefined result
Returning immediately instead of searching for boundary in modified versions
counterarguments: For small arrays (< 64 elements), linear search is often faster due to branch prediction and cache effects
evidence: Bisection method in mathematics is the continuous analog
Used in standard library implementations: std::binary_search, Java Collections.binarySearch

entries.title: Dynamic Programming: Memoization vs Tabulation
entries.claim: Dynamic programming solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure, using memoization (top-down with caching) or tabulation (bottom-up tabulation).
entries.solution: Two conditions: (1) Optimal substructure — optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems. (2) Overlapping subproblems — same subproblems solved repeatedly. Memoization: recursive + hash map/set/ array cache. Returns immediately if result cached. Tabulation: build table bottom-up, fill in order of increasing subproblem size. Both achieve same asymptotic improvement (e.g., Fibonacci O(n) vs naive O(2^n)).
assumptions: Problem has optimal substructure
Subproblems overlap sufficiently to benefit from caching
invariants: Memoized solutions must not have side effects in the cached function
Tabulation order must respect data dependencies (topological order)
Space-time tradeoff: tabulation can often be optimized to O(1) space by keeping only necessary rows
failure_modes: State explosion — too many parameters in state definition
Wrong state transition — missing transitions or including invalid states
Missing base cases — leads to infinite recursion or wrong answers
Integer overflow in counting problems — use big integers or modular arithmetic
counterarguments: Not all problems are amenable — if subproblems don't overlap, plain recursion may be clearer
evidence: Classic examples: Fibonacci, 0/1 Knapsack, Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, Coin Change

entries.title: Graph Traversal: BFS vs DFS
entries.claim: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores level-by-level using a queue, guaranteeing shortest path in unweighted graphs; Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as far as possible along each branch using a stack before backtracking.
entries.solution: Both O(V+E) time. BFS: FIFO queue, marks visited on enqueue, finds shortest path (unweighted). DFS: stack/recursion, marks visited on dequeue, detects cycles, topological sort, connected components. DFS can be implemented recursively (call stack) or iteratively (explicit stack). Post-order DFS yields topological sort reversal for DAGs.
assumptions: Graph fits in memory
Adjacency list representation for sparse graphs
invariants: Both visit every reachable node exactly once
BFS guarantees shortest path in unweighted graph
DFS finishes all nodes in a subtree before backtracking
failure_modes: Stack overflow with recursive DFS on deep graphs — use iterative with explicit stack
Not marking visited on enqueue (BFS) causes duplicate entries and exponential blowup
Missing visited check in directed graph with cycles causes infinite recursion
counterarguments: For shortest path in weighted graphs, BFS fails — use Dijkstra's algorithm instead
evidence: BFS used in social network friend suggestions, web crawling
DFS used in dependency resolution (topological sort), cycle detection (deadlock detection)

entries.title: SOLID Principles of Object-Oriented Design
entries.claim: SOLID is a set of five design principles that make object-oriented software more maintainable and scalable by reducing coupling and increasing cohesion.
entries.solution: S: Single Responsibility — one reason to change. O: Open/Closed — open for extension, closed for modification. L: Liskov Substitution — subtypes must be substitutable for their base types. I: Interface Segregation — many small interfaces better than one fat interface. D: Dependency Inversion — depend on abstractions, not concretions. Apply with dependency injection containers, use composition over inheritance.
assumptions: Codebase follows object-oriented paradigms
Interfaces/abstractions are stable enough to depend on
invariants: Each class should have one clear responsibility
Derived classes must not violate the behavior contract of the base class
High-level modules should not depend on low-level implementation details
failure_modes: Over-engineering with abstract base classes that are never extended
Violating LSP by throwing NotImplementedError in parent interface methods
Creating too many tiny interfaces that fragment the API
counterarguments: SOLID principles add complexity — for simple CRUD apps, YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) may be preferable
evidence: Robert C. Martin's 'Clean Code' and 'Agile Software Development' series
Java Spring framework embodies DI/IoC patterns
C# interfaces exemplify ISP

entries.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism and Thread Safety
entries.claim: Concurrency is about dealing with multiple tasks at once (interleaved execution), while parallelism is about executing multiple tasks simultaneously (multi-core); thread safety requires protecting shared mutable state.
entries.solution: Concurrency: single-core interleaving via multitasking (time-slicing, async/await). Parallelism: actual simultaneous execution on multiple cores. Thread safety primitives: (1) Mutex/monitor — mutual exclusion lock, one thread at a time. (2) Semaphore — allows N threads. (3) Read-Write lock — multiple readers, one writer. (4) Atomic operations — lock-free primitives (CAS). (5) Immutability — no locks needed if state never changes. (6) Thread-local storage — each thread has its own copy.
assumptions: Shared mutable state exists and must be protected
The programming language provides some concurrency primitives
invariants: At most one writer or multiple readers in critical section at a time (with RW-lock)
Deadlocks require 4 conditions — eliminate any one to prevent
Immutable objects are always thread-safe by definition
failure_modes: Deadlock — all 4 Coffman conditions met; prevent via lock ordering or timeout
Live starvation — thread perpetually denied access despite not being deadlocked
Race condition — read-modify-write not atomic, use compare-and-swap or synchronized block
counterarguments: Premature optimization of concurrency can introduce more bugs than it solves — start single-threaded, profile, then parallelize carefully
evidence: Amdahl's Law: speedup ≤ 1/(S + P/N) where S=serial fraction, P=parallel fraction, N=cores
Go channels and CSP model, Java synchronized/volatile/atomic, Rust borrow checker for compile-time safety

entries.title: Garbage Collection Algorithms
entries.claim: Garbage collection automatically reclaims memory occupied by objects no longer reachable, using tracing algorithms like reference counting, mark-and-sweep, copying, generational, or Mark-Compact collectors.
entries.solution: Reference counting: increment/decrement on reference change, free when count=0; fails on cycles. Mark-sweep: DFS/BFS from roots to mark live objects, sweep unmarked; causes fragmentation. Copying: copy live objects to new space, compact; wastes 50% space. Generational: young generation (minor GC, frequent, fast) + old generation (major GC, rare, slow); exploits infant mortality. Mark-compact: mark then compact live objects to eliminate fragmentation. G1 (Java), ZGC, Shenandoah minimize pause times via concurrency.
assumptions: Objects form a reachable graph from root set (stack, static fields)
Memory is sufficient to hold all live objects plus some overhead
invariants: Only unreachable objects can be safely collected
GC must not free objects still being referenced (must wait for safepoint)
Generational hypothesis: most objects die young
failure_modes: Stop-the-world pauses in non-concurrent collectors
Memory fragmentation in mark-sweep without compaction
Finalizer abuse — finalizers run unpredictably, can resurrect objects
Weak references needed for caches to avoid preventing GC
counterarguments: Manual memory management (C/C++) gives more predictable performance and lower memory usage in constrained environments
evidence: JVM HotSpot: Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC, Shenandoah collectors
Go: non-generational, non-moving, concurrent tri-color mark-sweep
Python: reference counting + cycle detector

entries.title: Observer Pattern and Pub/Sub
entries.claim: The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency where subjects notify registered observers of state changes, forming the basis of event-driven architectures and pub/sub systems.
entries.solution: Subject maintains a list of observers. register(observer) adds, unregister(observer) removes, notify() calls observer.update() on all. To avoid memory leaks from forgotten unregistration, use weak references or automatic GC. Pub/Sub generalizes this: publishers don't know subscribers; a broker/message queue routes messages (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis Pub/Sub). For UI frameworks: use reactive streams (RxJS, Kotlin Flow) with backpressure handling. Pull model: observer queries subject. Push model: subject pushes data to observer.
assumptions: Observers implement a known interface (update method)
Subjects and observers are in valid states for notification
invariants: Observers can register/unregister dynamically during notification (handle with copy-on-notify or proper synchronization)
Circular dependencies between observers can cause infinite loops
failure_modes: Memory leak from observers never unregistering
Concurrent modification exception during notify iteration
Event ordering guarantees lost in pub/sub with multiple partitions
counterarguments: For simple one-off notifications, direct method calls are simpler than observer infrastructure
evidence: Java's java.util.Observer (deprecated) and java.beans.PropertyChangeListener
RxJS Observable/Observer pattern
Android LiveData/StateFlow

entries.title: Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control
entries.claim: Dependency Injection (DI) is an IoC pattern where objects receive their dependencies from an external injector rather than creating them, reducing coupling and improving testability.
entries.solution: Three forms: (1) Constructor injection — dependencies as constructor params; recommended for required deps. (2) Setter/field injection — via property setter; for optional deps. (3) Interface injection — via interface method. DI containers manage lifecycle: singleton (one instance), scoped (one per request/transaction), transient (new each time). Service locator is an alternative but creates hidden dependencies. DI enables mocking in tests, loose coupling, and configuration externalization.
assumptions: Dependencies are defined as interfaces or abstractions
Container or factory can resolve concrete implementations
invariants: Dependencies should be injected at construction time for immutability
Circular dependencies must be resolved (pass-through constructor or redesign)
failure_modes: Service locator pattern hides dependencies — hard to trace and test
Over-injection — too many constructor params (>4) indicate violating single responsibility
Runtime dependency resolution failures when config is wrong
counterarguments: For small applications, manual new() is simpler than setting up a DI container framework
evidence: Spring Framework (Java), Dagger/Hilt (Android), .NET Core DI container, NestJS DI

entries.title: Immutability and Copy-on-Write
entries.claim: Immutable data structures cannot be modified after creation; copy-on-write (CoW) defers copying until a mutation is attempted, providing thread safety and predictable behavior at the cost of potential overhead.
entries.solution: Immutable: all fields final, no mutating methods, returns new instances on 'modification'. Benefits: thread safety, easy reasoning, caching/memoization, hash consistency. CoW: read operations access shared data, write operations copy-and-modify. Persistent data structures (Clojure, Haskell) use structural sharing to keep copies cheap. In multi-threaded contexts, immutability eliminates race conditions without locks. In UI frameworks, immutable state enables cheap change detection (React Redux).
assumptions: Memory for copies is affordable
Structural sharing is implemented for persistent collections
invariants: Immutable objects' hash codes can be cached indefinitely
References to immutable objects can be freely shared across threads
Deep immutability — all nested objects must also be immutable
failure_modes: Performance overhead from excessive copying without structural sharing
Using mutable objects inside an 'immutable' wrapper (e.g., mutable list field)
Forgetting to defensively copy mutable input parameters
counterarguments: For high-performance inner loops, mutable buffers are necessary; use functional style at API boundaries instead
evidence: React/Redux immutability for state diffing
Clojure's persistent data structures (vector, map, set)
Rust's ownership system enforces immutability by default

entries.title: HTTP: Status Codes and REST Principles
entries.claim: HTTP defines status code classes (1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error) and REST prescribes stateless, cacheable, uniform resource interactions via HTTP verbs.
entries.solution: Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created (POST success + Location header), 204 No Content (delete success), 301/302 (redirect), 304 Not Modified (conditional GET, cache hit), 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (needs auth), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict (concurrent modification/state conflict), 410 Gone (permanently removed), 429 Too Many Requests (retry-after), 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable (transient, retry with backoff). REST: stateless client-server, uniform interface (GET=read, POST=create, PUT=replace, PATCH=partial update, DELETE=delete), cacheable, layered, code-on-demand optional.
assumptions: Client and server communicate over HTTP/HTTPS
Resources are uniquely addressable via URI
invariants: GET must be safe and idempotent — no side effects
PUT is idempotent but not safe — same request repeated has same effect
DELETE is idempotent — multiple calls same as one
failure_modes: Returning 200 with an error body instead of proper error codes
POST for everything — loses HTTP semantic benefits
Not setting Cache-Control headers causing stale data
counterarguments: GraphQL intentionally breaks REST uniform interface for flexibility — trade-off is caching complexity
evidence: RFC 7231 (HTTP/1.1 semantics), RFC 7234 (caching), Roy Fielding's REST dissertation

entries.title: Idempotency in Distributed Systems
entries.claim: An operation is idempotent if applying it multiple times has the same effect as applying it once; critical for safe retries in distributed systems where network failures cause duplicate requests.
entries.solution: Mathematical definition: f(f(x)) = f(x). HTTP: GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST, PATCH are not. Implementation: (1) Idempotency key — client generates unique key, server stores {key: result} first time, returns cached result on repeat. (2) Deterministic operations — upsert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT), deterministic computation. (3) Check-then-act with conditional updates. Stripe, Shopify, AWS all support idempotency keys for payment/order APIs.
assumptions: Client can generate unique keys (UUID v4 or ULID)
Server can persist idempotency keys long enough for potential retries
invariants: Idempotency keys should expire (e.g., 24-72 hours)
Same idempotency key + same request body must be treated identically
failure_modes: Using different request bodies with the same idempotency key — server should reject or ignore
Idempotency key collision — use high-entropy UUIDs
Not cleaning up expired keys — storage bloat
counterarguments: Idempotency keys add storage overhead — for read-only operations, natural idempotency is better
evidence: Stripe API idempotency, AWS API idempotency tokens, HTTP RFC 9110 Section 9.2.2

entries.title: Event Loop: Concurrency Model
entries.claim: The event loop allows Node.js (and Python asyncio) to perform non-blocking I/O on a single thread by delegating operations to the system kernel and queuing callbacks when they complete.
entries.solution: Phases (Node.js): (1) Timers — setTimeout, setInterval callbacks. (2) Pending callbacks — I/O callbacks (deferred). (3) Idle/prepare — internal. (4) Poll — I/O events, new I/O data. (5) Check — setImmediate callbacks. (6) Close events. Call stack (synchronous), heap (objects), callback queue (completed async). Event loop: while(true) { check call stack empty; move from callback queue to call stack? }. Python asyncio: cooperative multitasking — await yields control; event loop schedules coroutines on ready queue. Microtasks (Promise.then, process.nextTick, asyncio callbacks) always run before macrotasks.
assumptions: Single-threaded execution model
OS provides non-blocking I/O via epoll/kqueue/IOCP
invariants: Microtasks run before the next event loop phase
Synchronous code blocks the entire event loop — keep callbacks fast
failure_modes: Blocking the event loop with synchronous CPU-heavy work
Uncaight async errors not caught by try/catch — use proper error handlers
Forgotten await causing silent async failures (floating promise)
counterarguments: For CPU-bound work, clustering (Node.js) or multi-processing (Python) is necessary — event loop alone cannot utilize multiple cores
evidence: Node.js official docs 'Event Loop' section, 'JavaScript Concurrency' by Nicholas C. Zakas
Python asyncio documentation and PEP 3156

domains.description: Timeless reliability, scalability, and distributed-systems design axioms applicable across all architectures.

entries.title: CAP Theorem and PACELC Extension
entries.claim: In a distributed system, you can only guarantee two of three properties: Consistency (all nodes see same data), Availability (every request gets a response), and Partition tolerance (system works despite network failures). PACELC extends this: if there's a partition, you choose CA; if not, you choose latency vs consistency.
entries.solution: CAP: network partitions are inevitable in distributed systems (network is not reliable). So you choose CA (not partition-tolerant, impractical) or CP (consistent + partition-tolerant, sacrifices availability during partition) or AP (available + partition-tolerant, sacrifices consistency). Real systems: CP — HBase, MongoDB, Etcd, Zookeeper; AP — DynamoDB, Cassandra, CouchDB, Couchbase. PACELC: P=partition, A=availability, C=consistency, E=else (normal operation), L=latency, C=consistency. ELC rule: else, choose Latency vs Consistency — e.g., Spanner chooses consistency, DynamoDB chooses latency.
assumptions: Network partitions are the only 'P' failure mode considered
Consistency means linearizability (strong consistency) in original formulation
invariants: Partition tolerance cannot be disabled in a distributed system
You cannot have all three: C + A + P simultaneously
failure_modes: Misunderstanding CAP — choosing CA in production (system fails entirely on network partition)
Confusing availability (responsive) with durability (data preserved)
Ignoring that single-node systems trivially satisfy CA
counterarguments: Brewer clarified CAP is not a hard guarantee — tunable consistency systems (Redis, Cosmos DB) offer intermediate choices
evidence: Gilbert & Lynch 2002 'Impossibility of Distributed Consensus'
Fox & Gurevin 2016 'PACELC: A Principled Discussion of Trade-offs in Distributed Systems'

invariants.title: Circuit Breaker Pattern
invariants.claim: The Circuit Breaker pattern prevents cascading failures by wrapping calls to external services with a proxy that trips open after repeated failures, temporarily stops requests, and probes to recover.
invariants.solution: Three states: (1) CLOSED — requests flow normally; failure counter increments; on reaching threshold (e.g., 5 consecutive failures), transitions to OPEN. (2) OPEN — requests immediately fail (fast-fail) without calling downstream; after timeout (e.g., 30s), transitions to HALF-OPEN. (3) HALF-OPEN — limited test requests; if success, CLOSE; if failure, back to OPEN. Reset failure count and timeout on success. Libraries: Netflix Hystrix (deprecated), Resilience4j, Polly (.NET), Sentinel (Alibaba).
assumptions: Failures are transient or temporary
Downstream service can recover
Monitoring is in place to alert on OPEN state
invariants: Half-open should allow only a limited number of test requests
Circuit breaker state must be thread-safe — concurrent accesses handled atomically
failure_modes: Threshold too low — trips on normal error fluctuations
Timeout too short — doesn't give downstream enough recovery time
invariants.failure_modes: Not setting a fallback response strategy — users see raw error
counterarguments: For critical internal services with guaranteed uptime, circuit breaker adds latency overhead
evidence: Netflix Hystrix documentation, Martin Fowler 'CircuitBreaker' article
Resilience4j documentation

invariants.title: Caching Strategies and Cache Invalidation
invariants.claim: Caching improves read performance but introduces cache invalidation, consistency, and stampede problems that must be carefully managed with correct strategies.
invariants.solution: Cache placement: (1) Client-side (browser), (2) Edge (CDN), (3) Application (Redis/Memcached), (4) Database (query cache). Invalidation: (1) Write-through — write to cache + DB atomically. (2) Write-around — write to DB, evict cache (avoids cache pollution). (3) Write-back (write-behind) — write to cache, async flush to DB (fastest but risk of data loss). (4) Cache-aside (lazy loading) — app checks cache, misses -> DB -> populate cache; most common. TTL strategies: fixed, sliding window, or version-based. Cache tags for selective invalidation. Cache stampede prevention: single-flight (deduplicate concurrent misses), stale-while-revalidate, read-through with locking.
assumptions: Data has temporal locality (frequently accessed)
Cache layer is highly available and fast (sub-millisecond)
invariants: Cache entry TTL should be set per data freshness requirements
Cache key should incorporate data version for atomic invalidation
failure_modes: Cache stampede — multiple requests miss simultaneously, overwhelming DB
Cache thundering herd — cache expiry causes mass DB load
Stale cache — serving outdated data without invalidation trigger
counterarguments: For write-heavy workloads, caching complexity exceeds benefits — consider read replicas instead
evidence: Redis documentation on caching patterns
Facebook's 'Achieving anoughness' paper on cache invalidation
Google's Site Reliability Engineering on cache management

invariants.title: Load Balancing Algorithms and Strategies
invariants.claim: Load balancers distribute traffic across backend servers using algorithms (round-robin, least connections, IP hash, weighted) and strategies (active/passive, L4/L7, health checks) for high availability and scalability.
invariants.solution: Layer 4 (transport) vs Layer 7 (application/HTTP) balancing. Algorithms: (1) Round Robin (weighted) — simple, good for homogeneous servers. (2) Least Connections — sends to server with fewest active connections; better for long-lived connections. (3) IP Hash — sticky sessions by client IP; consistent hashing for distributed cache sessions. (4) Least Response Time — server with lowest average response time. (5) Weighted Round Robin for unequal server capacity. Sticky sessions: needed for stateful apps but reduces resilience (server failure loses session unless replicated). Health checks: active (periodic probe) and passive (monitor failed requests). Failover: hot standby + health check + graceful drain.
assumptions: Servers are roughly homogeneous in capacity
Health checks are reliable and not too expensive
invariants: Health check interval should be shorter than client timeout
Graceful shutdown must drain connections before terminating server
failure_modes: Sticky session loss on server failure (session not replicated)
Health check too aggressive — false positive marks healthy server down
Uneven weight distribution due to misconfigured connection counting
counterarguments: For very high request rates, DNS-level load balancing (anycast) with BGP may be simpler than L7 proxies
evidence: NGINX, HAProxy, AWS ALB/NLB documentation
Google SRE Workbook on load balancing

invariants.title: Database Sharding and Partitioning
invariants.claim: Sharding and partitioning horizontally scale databases by splitting data into smaller independent pieces (shards/partitions) based on a shard key, enabling horizontal scaling across machines while maintaining query performance.
invariants.solution: Partitioning (single machine): horizontal (rows split by range/list/hash) vs vertical (columns split). Sharding (multiple machines): (1) Range-based — sequential ranges (date, ID); easy but hot spots. (2) Hash-based — consistent hashing; even distribution but range queries need all shards. (3) Directory-based — lookup table maps key to shard. Shard key must: (a) have high cardinality, (b) avoid hot spots, (c) group related data (co-location). Cross-shard transactions need two-phase commit (2PC) or eventual consistency + saga pattern. Rebalancing: split hotspots, merge underutilized shards. Use connection pool per shard + shard router.
assumptions: Shard key distributes data evenly
Applications can route queries to correct shard with minimal overhead
invariants: Shard key is immutable — changing it requires re-sharding the row
Cross-shard joins/transactions have higher latency and complexity
failure_modes: Hot shard — uneven key distribution causes overload on one shard
Shard key too granular — excessive scatter-gather queries
Uneven shard sizes require frequent rebalancing
counterarguments: For most applications, vertical scaling + read replicas + caching covers needs without sharding complexity
evidence: by Martin Kleppmann — Chapter 6 on partitioning/sharding
MongoDB sharding documentation
MySQL partitioning

invariants.title: The Twelve-Factor App Methodology
invariants.claim: The Twelve-Factor methodology defines the canonical way to build SaaS applications that can scale as a service, covering codebase, dependencies, config, backing services, build/release/run, processes, port binding, concurrency, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs, and admin processes.
invariants.solution: 1. Codebase — one codebase, many deploys. 2. Dependencies — explicit, pinned, isolated. 3. Config — environment variables (never in code). 4. Backing services — attached resources (DB, cache, queues). 5. Build/Release/Run — separate stages. 6. Processes — stateless, shared-nothing. 7. Port binding — self-contained service listening on port. 8. Concurrency — scale out via processes. 9. Disposability — fast start/stop, graceful shutdown. 10. Dev/Prod parity — minimal gap. 11. Logs — event stream. 12. Admin processes — one-off, run in prod environment via release phase.
assumptions: Application is deployed as a service (cloud-native)
Dependencies are managed via package managers
invariants: Processes are stateless and share nothing — state stored in backing services
Config varies by deploy, never per-environment in codebase
failure_modes: Treating admin processes as special — should use same environment as app processes
Storing state in process memory — breaks on restart and with multiple instances
counterarguments: Some factors (logs, admin processes) may be better handled by infrastructure than app code
evidence: 12factor.net — canonical reference, used by Heroku, Cloud Foundry, and modern platform engineering

invariants.title: Backpressure in Reactive Systems
invariants.claim: Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow consumer signals to a fast producer that it should slow down data production to prevent overwhelming buffers and causing system failure.
invariants.solution: Without backpressure: fast producer fills unbounded buffer → OOM crash or latency spike. Strategies: (1) Bounded buffers — producer blocks when full. (2) Dropping — drop new/old messages (with metrics). (3) Buffering with size limit. (4) Explicit signal — consumer sends ACK to producer. (5) Rate limiting — producer throttles via tokens/semaphore. (6) Pull-based — consumer requests next item explicitly. Reactive Streams spec mandates backpressure. In microservices: circuit breaker + retry + queue depth monitoring. TCP implements backpressure via sliding window.
assumptions: System has measurable processing rates for producer and consumer
Consumer can emit backpressure signal to producer
invariants: Buffer size must be bounded to prevent unbounded memory growth
Backpressure must propagate end-to-end, not just one hop
failure_modes: Producer ignores backpressure signal — data loss or OOM
Backpressure propagates too aggressively — system throughput collapses
Deadlock when backpressure and flow control interact
counterarguments: For fire-and-forget logging, dropping with a counter is acceptable instead of backpressure
evidence: Reactive Streams specification (java.util.concurrent.Flow)
Akka Streams backpressure documentation

invariants.title: Consensus Algorithms: Paxos and Raft
invariants.claim: Paxos and Raft are consensus algorithms that allow a distributed system to agree on a single value despite node failures, using leader election, log replication, and quorum-based commitment.
invariants.solution: Problem: N nodes, some may fail (stop, crash, Byzantine). Goal: agree on a sequence of commands. Paxos (hard to understand): proposer -> acceptor -> learner; quorum majority; multi-Paxos for log. Raft (designed for understandability): (1) Leader election — randomized timer, candidate requests votes, majority wins. (2) Log replication — leader receives command, appends to log, replicates to followers, commits when majority acks. (3) Safety — leader must have up-to-date log (candidate wins only if up-to-date). (4) Membership changes — joint consensus. (5) Read index optimization for linearizable reads without log writes.
assumptions: Non-Byzantine (crash-stop) failure model
Majority of nodes are available and can communicate
invariants: Leader can only be elected if its log is at least as up-to-date as the voter's log
A log entry is committed once replicated on majority
failure_modes: Split vote — no candidate gets majority; resolved by randomized election intervals
Stale read from leader that was deposed — use read index/heartbeat
Log inconsistency — follower's log diverges from leader; resolved by overwriting
counterarguments: For systems tolerating Byzantine failures, use PBFT or Tendermint instead of Raft
evidence: Ongaro & Ousterhout 'In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm' (Raft, 2014)
Lamport 'Paxos Made Simple' (2001)

invariants.title: Saga Pattern for Distributed Transactions
invariants.claim: The Saga pattern manages distributed transactions by breaking them into a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that rolls back on failure, avoiding the complexity and performance cost of two-phase commit.
invariants.solution: Two coordination styles: (1) Choreography — each service emits events; when a saga step completes, it publishes an event; the next service consumes it and executes its local transaction + publishes the next event. If a step fails, publish a compensation event. Service listens for compensation events and reverses its action. (2) Orchestration — a saga orchestrator (central coordinator) sends commands to each service; services execute and return results; orchestrator decides next step or triggers compensating transactions. Compensation actions must be idempotent. Example: transfer money — create debit, create credit, if credit fails → compensate debit. Saga patterns require careful design of compensating actions and idempotency.
assumptions: Each local transaction either fully succeeds or fails
Compensating actions are available for every step
invariants: Compensating actions are idempotent — must handle being executed multiple times
Saga steps are eventually consistent — intermediate inconsistent states may be observable
failure_modes: Irreversible actions in saga — can't be compensated (e.g., sent email)
Race condition — two compensating actions for same resource conflict
Partial failures leave system in inconsistent state if compensation also fails
counterarguments: For simple 2-database transactions, two-phase commit or XA may be simpler than a full saga choreography
evidence: Garcia-Molina & Salem 'The Saga Pattern' (1987)
Microservices Patterns by Chris Richardson — Saga chapter

entries.description: Evergreen AI/ML theory — concepts that do not change with model releases. Core to maintaining knowledge when external LLM providers are down.

entries.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
entries.claim: The bias-variance tradeoff describes the tension between model simplicity (high bias, underfitting) and model complexity (high variance, overfitting) in minimizing total prediction error.
entries.solution: Total Error = Bias^2 + Variance + Irreducible Error (noise). Bias — error from erroneous assumptions in the learning algorithm (underfitting). Variance — error from sensitivity to fluctuations in training data (overfitting). Irreducible — error from noise/no way to improve. To reduce bias: add complexity, more features, fewer constraints. To reduce variance: more training data, regularization, ensemble methods, cross-validation. The sweet spot minimizes total error.
assumptions: The learning algorithm can express the true relationship given enough capacity
Training and test data are drawn from the same distribution
invariants: Increasing model complexity generally reduces bias but increases variance
Ensemble averaging reduces variance without affecting bias
failure_modes: Confusing variance (model sensitivity) with irreducible error (noise)
Not collecting more data as the primary variance-reduction lever
Hyperparameter tuning without cross-validation — overfitting to validation set
counterarguments: Modern deep learning with massive data shows the tradeoff plane shifting — more data + compute often reduces both bias and variance
evidence: Geman et al. 'A connectionist approach to cognitive breakdown' (1992)
Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman 'The Elements of Statistical Learning'

entries.title: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
entries.claim: RAG combines a retriever that searches external documents with a generator (LLM) that conditions its output on retrieved passages, reducing hallucination and providing source attribution without model fine-tuning.
entries.solution: Pipeline: (1) Index — document chunker splits docs into passages, each embedded into dense vectors (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, bge-m3, etc.) stored in a vector DB (Chroma, pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate). (2) Query — user query embedded, similarity search (cosine/ dot product) retrieves top-k passages. (3) Rerank — cross-encoder (ColBERT, Cohere reranker) refines relevance beyond semantic search. (4) Generate — passages concatenated as context, LLM generates answer with citation prompt. Variants: naive RAG (single retrieval), Fusion RAG (query rewrite + multiple retrievers), Self-RAG (LLM self-refines). For hallucination reduction: prompt to cite, use grounding-passage attention, or self-critique.
assumptions: Retrieved passages are relevant and correct
Embedding model generalizes to query domain
invariants: Passage chunks should be small enough (200-500 tokens) for precise retrieval
RAG cannot correct errors in the indexed documents — garbage in, garbage out
failure_modes: Hallucination despite retrieval — LLM ignores context or generates unsupported claims
Low recall — retrieval misses relevant documents due to embedding mismatch
Citation fabrication — LLM cites documents not in the retrieved set
counterarguments: For factual Q&A over well-structured data, a fine-tuned retriever + LLM may outperform generic dense retrieval
evidence: Lewis et al. 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP' (2020)
SupremeAI's own RAGPipeline in backend/memory/rag_pipeline.py

entries.title: Loss Functions and Their Use Cases
entries.claim: Selecting the appropriate loss function is critical for model performance — classification uses cross-entropy, regression uses MSE/MAE, and specialized losses (contrastive, focal, triplet) address specific challenges like class imbalance or embedding learning.
entries.solution: Classification: Cross-entropy (binary — sigmoid + BCE, multi-class — softmax + CE). Focal loss (down-weights easy negatives) for class imbalance. Regression: MSE (L2, sensitive to outliers), MAE (L1, robust to outliers), Huber (smooth L1, combines both). Ranking/embedding: Contrastive loss (pull similar, push dissimilar), Triplet loss (anchor, positive, negative margins), InfoNCE (contrastive with noise contrastive estimation). Regularization: L1 (sparsity), L2 (weight decay). Custom: combine multiple losses with weights. For LLMs: next-token cross-entropy is standard; label smoothing + dropout as regularizer.
assumptions: Loss function is differentiable (or sub-differentiable)
Optimization target aligns with business metric
invariants: Loss should be non-negative and zero at perfect prediction (for distance-based losses)
For gradient-based optimization, loss must be continuous in model parameters
failure_modes: Mismatched loss and metric — minimizing CE may not maximize F1
Numerical instability — use log-sum-exp trick, clamp predictions
Outliers dominate MSE — prefer MAE or Huber
counterarguments: For some tasks (e.g., ranking), learning-to-rank losses (LambdaRank, ListNet) may outperform pointwise losses
evidence: Goodfellow et al. 'Deep Learning' — Chapter 6 on regularization, Chapter 8 on optimization
Focal Loss paper (Lin et al. CVPR 2017)

entries.title: Gradient Descent and Modern Optimizers
entries.claim: Gradient descent optimizes model parameters by iteratively moving opposite to the gradient of the loss, with momentum, adaptive learning rates, and weight decay improving convergence speed and stability.
entries.solution: Vanilla GD: θ = θ - lr * ∇L(θ). SGD with momentum: v = βv + (1-β)∇L; θ = θ - lr * v; smooths oscillations, speeds convergence in relevant direction. Adam: maintains per-parameter first moment (mean) and second moment (uncentered variance); bias-corrected; lr_t = lr * sqrt(1-β2^t)/(1-β1^t). AdamW: decoupled weight decay (L2 regularization applied directly to parameters, not through loss). LAMB/LARS: layer-wise adaptive learning for large-batch training. Adafactor: memory-efficient (no second moment buffer). Gradient clipping prevents exploding gradients.
assumptions: Loss function is smooth (Lipschitz continuous gradient)
Learning rate is carefully tuned per model/dataset
invariants: For SGD convergence, learning rate must satisfy Robbins-Monro conditions (∑lr=∞, ∑lr^2 < ∞)
Adam's epsilon prevents division by zero in second moment
failure_modes: Learning rate too high — diverges or oscillates
Learning rate too low — slow convergence/stuck in saddle point
Adam converges to sharp minimum — may generalize worse than SGD
counterarguments: For convex problems, plain SGD with momentum may be more reliable than adaptive methods
evidence: Kingma & Ba 'Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization' (2015)
Loshchilov & Hutter 'Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization' (2019)

entries.title: Machine Learning Evaluation Metrics
entries.claim: Correct metric selection ensures models optimize the right objective — classification uses accuracy/precision/recall/F1/AUROC, regression uses MAE/MSE/RMSE/R², ranking uses NDCG/MRR, and generation uses BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR or human evaluation.
entries.solution: Classification: Accuracy = (TP+TN)/total; Precision = TP/(TP+FP); Recall = TP/(TP+FN); F1 = 2*P*R/(P+R). Use F1 when classes are imbalanced; AUROC for overall ranking ability; AUPRC when positive class is rare. Regression: MAE (robust), MSE (penalizes outliers more), RMSE (interpretable in target units), R² (variance explained, can be negative). MAPE (relative error %; undefined at zero). NDCG (ranking quality at k), MRR (reciprocal rank of first relevant). For LLM generation: BLEU/ROGUE n-gram overlap (cheap but imperfect), BERTScore/BLEURT (embedding-based), human eval (gold standard for quality/helpfulness/harmfulness).
assumptions: Test set is representative of production data
Metrics align with business objectives
invariants: Always evaluate on a held-out test set never used in training or validation
Use stratified sampling for imbalanced classification
failure_modes: Accuracy is misleading for imbalanced datasets (>99% negative → 99% accuracy trivially)
Overfitting to a single metric — optimize multiple complementary metrics
Data leakage between train/test splits (time-based or row-based
counterarguments: For ranking/search systems, offline metrics (NDCG) may not correlate with user engagement — supplement with A/B tests
evidence: Saito & Rehmsmeier 'The precision-recall plot' (2005)
Manning 'Evaluation in IR' (2020)

entries.title: Tokenization Methods and Tokenizer Types
entries.claim: Tokenization converts text into tokens for LLM consumption; subword methods (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece) balance vocabulary size and sequence length, with BPE handling unknown words gracefully.
entries.solution: Word-level: simple but large vocab + OOV problem. Character-level: tiny vocab but long sequences, poor semantic grouping. Subword: (1) Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) — iteratively merges most frequent token pairs; used by GPT-2/3/4. (2) WordPiece — similar to BPE but uses likelihood-based merging; used by BERT. (3) SentencePiece/Unigram — probabilistic, can sample; used by T5, ALBERT. (4) Byte-level BPE — operates on bytes (256 base vocab), handles any character; used by GPT-NeoX. Tokenizer size affects: 1 token ≈ 4 chars (English). Multilingual tokenizers need larger vocab (e.g., 250k for mBERT vs 30k for English-only).
assumptions: Text is encoded in a consistent encoding (UTF-8)
Tokenizer aligns with model training vocabulary
invariants: Same tokenizer must be used for training and inference — mismatched tokenization silently degrades model performance
Tokenization is not perfectly reversible — whitespace and formatting may be lost
failure_modes: Using wrong tokenizer (e.g., GPT-2 tokenizer with BERT model) — token IDs mean different embeddings
Not adding special tokens (BOS/EOS/SEP/PAD) — model doesn't know sequence boundaries
Unknown tokens — OOV words become [UNK] or arbitrary subwords
counterarguments: For some languages (Chinese, Japanese), word segmentation adds complexity that subword tokenizers partially solve
evidence: GPT-2: Radford et al. 'Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners'
SentencePiece: Kudo 'SentencePiece' (2018)

entries.title: Transformer Architecture: Attention and Positional Encoding
entries.claim: Transformers use self-attention to compute contextual representations of input tokens in parallel (vs sequential RNNs), with multi-head attention capturing different relation types and positional encodings providing sequence order.
entries.solution: Self-attention: attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V. Q/K/V from linear projections of input. Multi-head: h attention heads in parallel, concatenated + projected — captures different relation types. Encoder: multi-head attention + FFN (2 linear + GELU) + residual + layer norm (pre-norm or post-norm). Decoder: same + masked self-attention (prevent peeking) + encoder-decoder attention. Layer norm: normalizes across feature dim, more stable than batch norm for variable seq lengths. Positional encoding: sinusoidal (PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos/10000^(2i/d_model))) — allows extrapolation. Alternatives: learned positional embeddings (BERT), rotary (RoPE) for rotary position embedding (GPT-J, LLaMA), ALiBi (linear bias).
assumptions: Input sequence length fits in model's context window
Attention mechanism is the dominant computational cost
invariants: Attention weights sum to 1 (softmax row-normalized)
Self-attention is permutation-invariant without positional encoding
failure_modes: Quadratic memory/compute in sequence length — use linear attention (Performer, Linformer) or sparse attention for long context
Not scaling attention scores (missing 1/sqrt(d_k)) — gradients explode at initialization
Positional encoding not applied at inference if missing at training time
counterarguments: For some tasks (copying, sorting), RNNs may generalize better than transformers due to stronger inductive bias
evidence: Vaswani et al. 'Attention Is All You Need' (2017)
RoFormer: Su et al. 'RoFormer' (2021)
ALiBi: Press et al. 'Train Short, Test Long' (2022)

entries.title: Sampling Methods for LLM Text Generation
entries.claim: Text generation sampling strategies (greedy, temperature, top-k, top-p/nucleus, typical) control output diversity and quality, with the choice depending on the task (deterministic extraction vs creative generation).
entries.solution: Greedy: pick argmax — deterministic, repetitive, misses alternatives. Temperature sampling: softmax(logits/temperature) — low T=0.1 (focused/deterministic), high T=1.5 (diverse/random). Top-k: restrict to k highest-probability tokens, sample from subset. Top-p (nucleus): restrict to smallest set with cumulative prob >= p (e.g., 0.9), more adaptive than fixed k. Typical sampling: tokens near expected frequency. Repetition penalty: divides logits of already-generated tokens. Frequency/count penalties: reduce logit proportional to occurrence count. Best practice: temperature 0.2-0.7 for factual, 0.7-1.0 for creative; top_p 0.9-1.0; enable presence penalty.
assumptions: Logits represent well-calibrated probability distribution
Vocabulary is fixed and known at inference
invariants: Greedy decoding and temperature 0 produce identical output
Top-k=1 is equivalent to greedy decoding
failure_modes: Temperature too high (T > 2.0) — incoherent, off-topic output
Top-k too small — misses relevant but lower-ranked tokens
No repetition penalty — generates repetitive text loops
counterarguments: Beam search can produce more globally coherent text than sampling for some tasks (translation, summarization)
evidence: Holtzman et al. 'The Curious Case of Neural Text Generation' (2020) — nucleus sampling paper
OpenAI GPT-3 API documentation on sampling parameters

entries.description: Evergreen security axioms, OWASP categories, cryptography fundamentals — critical for system resilience when external security services are down.

entries.title: OWASP Top 10: Security Risks Classification
entries.claim: OWASP Top 10 enumerates the most critical web application security risks, updated periodically based on developer survey data, providing a prioritization framework for application security.
entries.solution: Current (2021) Top 10: (1) Broken Access Control — users access unauthorized resources (IDOR, BOLA). Fix: deny-by-default, check on every request. (2) Cryptographic Failures (formerly Sensitive Data Exposure) — weak crypto, plaintext storage. Fix: TLS 1.3, AES-256, proper hashing (bcrypt/Argon2). (3) Injection — SQLi, command injection, LDAP injection. Fix: parameterized queries, ORM, input validation, allowlist. (4) Insecure Design — missing security in SDLC. Fix: threat modeling, secure design patterns. (5) Security Misconfiguration — default creds, verbose errors, debug mode. Fix: hardening, least privilege. (6) Vulnerable Components — outdated deps. Fix: SCA, dependency scanning (safety, pip-audit, Snyk). (7) Auth Failures — session fixation, weak passwords. Fix: MFA, session rotation, secure cookies. (8) Data Integrity Failures — unsigned data. Fix: signatures. (9) Logging Failures — no monitoring. Fix: structured logging, SIEM. (10) SSRF — server-side request forgery. Fix: URL allowlist, egress filtering.
assumptions: Application has input validation layer
Security is considered throughout SDLC, not just at deployment
invariants: Never trust user input — validate, sanitize, encode for output context
Defense in depth — multiple independent controls
failure_modes: OWASP-only mindset — checklist compliance without deep threat modeling
Blocking only SQL but missing NoSQL injection in same code path
Fixing symptoms (input sanitization) instead of root cause (parameterized queries)
counterarguments: For internal tools with no internet exposure, some OWASP categories may be lower priority
evidence: OWASP.org Top 10 (2021), cheat sheets, testing guide
MITRE CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Errors

entries.title: Encryption: Symmetric, Asymmetric, and Hash Functions
entries.claim: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key (fast, for bulk data), asymmetric uses public/private key pairs (slow, for key exchange and signatures), and cryptographic hash functions provide one-way integrity verification.
entries.solution: Symmetric: AES (advanced encryption standard, 128/256-bit key, block cipher, modes: GCM for authenticated encryption, CBC for compatibility, CTR for streaming). ChaCha20-Poly1305 for mobile/embedded (faster than AES without hardware AES). Key exchange: Diffie-Hellman (DH) or ECDH over named curves (secp256r1/P-256, X25519). Signatures: RSA-PSS/RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 (legacy), ECDSA (smaller signatures), Ed25519 (EdDSA, fast, deterministic nonces — preferred). Hashing: SHA-256/384/512 (SHA-2 family), SHA-3 (Keccak, different construction). Password hashing: bcrypt (GPU-resistant, built-in salt), scrypt (memory-hard, tunable N/r/p), Argon2id (winner of PHC, memory + time + parallelism params). NEVER use MD5 or SHA-1 for security.
assumptions: Cryptographically secure random number generation available (os.urandom, /dev/urandom)
Keys have sufficient entropy (≥128 bits)
invariants: Never reuse nonce/IV with same AES key + GCM mode — leads to catastrophic failure
Never use the same RSA key for encryption and signing
failure_modes: Hardcoding keys/secrets in source code or config files
Using deterministic random (not CSPRNG) for cryptographic operations
Weak/legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, RC4, DES) still in production
Reusing nonce with stream cipher — attacker can XOR ciphertexts to recover plaintext
counterarguments: For maximum performance in trusted environments, symmetric-only encryption may suffice if key exchange is handled by network layer
evidence: NIST FIPS 197 (AES), NIST SP 800-57 (key management)
RFC 8439 HMAC+AES-GCM, RFC 8032 EdDSA
Password Hashing Competition (PHC) winner: Argon2

entries.title: Secure Authentication and Session Management
entries.claim: Secure authentication requires multi-factor verification, password hashing with slow algorithms, secure session tokens, and proper session lifecycle management to prevent account takeover and session hijacking.
entries.solution: Password storage: bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2id with per-user salt; cost factor high enough (bcrypt cost ≥12, Argon2id t=3, m=64MB). Never store plaintext or MD5/SHA. MFA: TOTP (RFC 6238) or WebAuthn/FIDO2 (passwordless). Session management: (1) Use cryptographically random session IDs (≥128 bits), httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies. (2) Generate new session ID on login (session fixation prevention). (3) Regenerate on privilege escalation. (4) Set expiration + sliding timeout. (5) Destroy on logout server-side. (6) Token rotation for refresh tokens (each refresh rotates both access and refresh token). JWT: use RS256/HS256, never trust client-side claims, short expiry (≤15 min), refresh via secure refresh token. OAuth2: PKCE for public clients.
assumptions: TLS (HTTPS) is enforced end-to-end
Clock synchronization for TOTP (RFC 6238 allows ±1 step window)
invariants: Session ID must be unpredictable (CSPRNG) and ≥128 bits
Password reset links must be one-time use and time-limited
failure_modes: Session fixation — attacker-provided session ID accepted instead of regenerated
JWT stored in localStorage — XSS can steal token; prefer HttpOnly cookies
Not invalidating refresh tokens on logout/revocation
Password reset allows enumerating accounts via different messages
counterarguments: For internal tools with SSO (SAML/OIDC), custom auth implementation is unnecessary and adds risk
evidence: OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet, OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet
NIST SP 800-63B Digital Identity Guidelines
RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7519 (JWT)

failure_modes.title: Injection Attacks and Prevention
failure_modes.claim: Injection attacks occur when untrusted data is interpreted as part of a command/query language; prevention requires parameterized queries, input validation with allowlists, and context-specific output encoding.
failure_modes.solution: SQL Injection: use parameterized queries (prepared statements) or ORM; never string-concatenate user input into SQL. Example: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s', (user_id,)) vs f-string. NoSQL injection: validate types (parseInt), use ORM, avoid loose equality (== in JS). Command injection: avoid shell=True in subprocess (Python), use argument lists; allowlist permitted commands. LDAP injection: parameterized filters. XPath injection: avoid string building, use parameterized. Template injection (SSTI): sandboxed template engine (Jinja2 autoescape, Twig), don't render user input as template. General prevention: (1) Allowlist validation (not blocklist). (2) Output encoding (HTML escape in HTML context, JS escape in JS context). (3) Context-specific: HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, CSS, URL. (4) CSP headers as defense-in-depth.
assumptions: Input validation libraries are used consistently across the codebase
Output encoding matches the target context (HTML, JS, URL, CSS)
invariants: Parameterization is the primary defense — validation is secondary
All user-derived output must be encoded for its output context
failure_modes: Allowlist regex too permissive (e.g., a-zA-Z0-9] without length limit)
Using blocklist instead of allowlist — attacker finds bypass
Encoding for wrong context (HTML-encode JS that needs JS-encoding
counterarguments: For legacy code with extensive string concatenation, parameterized query refactoring may require careful migration planning
evidence: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — SQL injection and XSS labs
OWASP Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
CWE-89 (SQL injection), CWE-79 (XSS)

failure_modes.title: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) Prevention
failure_modes.claim: SSRF occurs when a server fetches a user-supplied URL without validation, allowing attackers to access internal services, cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), and private networks.
failure_modes.solution: Defense layers: (1) URL allowlist — only permit approved domains. (2) IP address resolution — resolve to IP, check against private ranges (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, 127.x, 169.254.x, ::1, fc00::/7). Block DNS rebinding — resolve twice at different times. (3) Redirect validation — follow redirects but re-validate the final URL against allowlist and IP checks. (4) Egress filtering — firewall blocks outbound to internal networks/metadata. (5) Cloud-specific: IAM role with minimal permissions, block access to metadata service. (6) Use a proxy/via service (e.g., Google's GSB, AWS PrivateLink) for controlled outbound. Library-level: use httpx/requests with custom adapter, or a dedicated SSRF-safe HTTP client.
assumptions: Attacker can manipulate the URL parameter in at least one endpoint
Applications sometimes need to fetch arbitrary external URLs
invariants: DNS resolution and connection must both be validated
Redirects must re-pass all validation checks
failure_modes: Only validating initial URL but not following redirects — 302 to metadata endpoint
counterarguments: For applications that legitimately proxy arbitrary URLs (e.g., screenshot services), defense-in-depth with network-level controls is essential but user-level blocking may be impractical
evidence: PortSwigger Web Security Academy SSRF labs
Google Cloud SSRF best practices documentation

entries.description: SQL, database modeling, ETL, and transaction patterns that remain constant regardless of database vendor.

entries.title: SQL Indexing Strategies: B-Tree, Hash, GiST, GIN, BRIN
entries.claim: Database indexes trade faster reads for slower writes and additional storage; B-tree is the default for most queries, while specialized indexes (hash, GiST, GIN, BRIN) address specific data types and query patterns.
entries.solution: B-tree (balanced tree) — default for =, <>, <, >, <=, >=, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE (prefix). Works on any sortable type. Good clustering effect. Hash — only =, fast O(1), but no ordering, no prefix queries, not crash-safe (rebuild after crash). GiST (Generalized Search Tree) — for geometric, full-text, range, IP, JSONB path. GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) — for arrays, full-text, JSONB keys; fast lookup but large. BRIN (Block Range) — for very large append-only/sequential tables (time-series); small storage, fast enough for range queries at scale. Index creation cost: B-tree moderate, GIN high (must index every element), BRIN low. Partial indexes — index only WHERE condition (e.g., active rows only) saves space and write cost.
assumptions: Table has sufficient data volume to benefit from indexing
Write load justifies read speed improvement
invariants: Every index adds write overhead — CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in production
Postgres: one index per table is recommended for FK constraints
failure_modes: Too many indexes — slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
Composite index column order matters — leftmost prefix rule
Index on frequently updated column — high write cost with minimal read benefit
counterarguments: For very small tables (< 1000 rows), sequential scan may be faster than indexed lookup
evidence: PostgreSQL documentation 'Database Physical Storage' and 'Indexes' chapter
Use-The-Index-Luke.com by Markus Winand

entries.title: Database Transactions: ACID and Isolation Levels
entries.claim: Database transactions ensure ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) with four isolation levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable) that trade off concurrency for correctness by preventing concurrency anomalies.
entries.solution: ACID: (1) Atomicity — all-or-nothing; ROLLBACK undoes. (2) Consistency — valid state transitions; constraints enforced. (3) Isolation — concurrent transactions see consistent snapshot. (4) Durability — committed persists after crash (WAL/f syncs). Isolation levels and anomalies they prevent: Read Uncommitted — dirty reads (uncommitted data visible). Read Committed — prevents dirty reads; allows non-repeatable reads (row changes between reads) and phantom reads (rows appear/disappear). Repeatable Read — prevents dirty + non-repeatable; allows phantom (in SQL Server, prevents phantom in PostgreSQL). Serializable — prevents all three (snapshot isolation in Postgres, predicate locks in SQL Server). Implementation: PostgreSQL uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) for snapshot isolation; writes use locks. Two-phase locking (2PL) in MySQL/InnoDB.
assumptions: Database implements at least Read Committed by default
Application can tolerate the concurrency limitations of higher isolation levels
invariants: Serializable is correct but slowest — use lowest level that prevents your anomalies
MVCC avoids read locks but still needs write locks for mutations
failure_modes: Using Read Committed expecting consistency — non-repeatable reads cause logic bugs
Serializable snapshot isolation can cause serialization failures — app must retry
Long-running transactions in PostgreSQL prevent vacuum — bloat increases, autovacuum can't reclaim
counterarguments: For analytical workloads, eventual consistency with read replicas may be acceptable instead of strong consistency
evidence: PostgreSQL documentation on MVCC and isolation levels
ANSI SQL-92 standard on isolation
Jim Gray 'The Transaction Concept' — ACID paper

invariants.title: Database Normalization and Denormalization Trade-offs
invariants.claim: Normalization eliminates redundancy by decomposing tables into related entities with normal forms (1NF through 5NF), while denormalization intentionally introduces redundancy for read performance, trading storage and consistency complexity for query speed.
invariants.solution: Normal forms: (1NF — atomic values. (2) 2NF — no partial dependency on subset of composite PK. (3) 3NF — no transitive dependency. (4) BCNF — every determinant is a candidate key. (5) 4NF — no multi-valued dependencies. (6) 5NF — no join dependencies. Denormalization strategies: (1) Pre-computed materialized views/aggregates. (2) Denormalized columns (copy name into orders table to avoid JOIN). (3) Storing derived/calculated data. (4) Using array/JSON columns for one-to-many. (5) Wide tables (columnar for analytics). Trade-off: denormalization speeds reads but complicates writes (must maintain consistency across redundant copies). Use database triggers, background jobs, or application-level cascade to keep denormalized data in sync. Data warehouses intentionally denormalize (star/snowflake schema).
assumptions: Read-heavy workload justifies write-side complexity
Schema evolution is manageable with migrations
invariants: Every denormalized field must have a clear update strategy (trigger/event/invalidate cache)
Normalized data is the source of truth; denormalized copies are derived
failure_modes: Inconsistent data across denormalized copies — stale reads
Over-normalization — excessive joins making queries slow and complex
Forgetting to update denormalized copy in one write path — silent data corruption
counterarguments: For OLTP systems with mixed read/write workloads, a balance of normalization (3NF) + selective denormalization (frequently queried columns) is optimal
evidence: Date 'An Introduction to Database Systems'
Kimball vs Inmon data warehouse modeling approaches

invariants.title: ETL/ELT Pipeline Design Patterns
invariants.claim: ETL (Extract-Transform-Load) transforms data before loading, while ELT loads raw data first then transforms; the choice depends on compute location and data volume, with idempotent pipelines and incremental processing as key design principles.
invariants.solution: ETL: extract from source (API/database/stream), transform in staging (clean, filter, enrich, aggregate), load to warehouse. Good for: small/medium data, on-prem → cloud. ELT: extract, load raw to warehouse, transform using warehouse compute (SQL). Good for: cloud warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift), large data. Idempotent: same input → same output; use deterministic IDs, upsert (INSERT...ON CONFLICT), checkpoint tracking (watermark column). Incremental: (1) Timestamp watermark — process new rows since last watermark. (2) CDC (Change Data Capture) — capture inserts/updates/deletes via database log. (3) Batch + micro-batch. (4) Stream (Kafka, Kinesis, Pub/Sub). Error handling: dead letter queue (DLQ), retry with exponential backoff, circuit breaker. Monitoring: freshness (data lag), row counts (input vs output), volume (anomalies).
assumptions: Source data has a reliable way to track what's new (timestamp, CDC log, cursor)
Warehouse compute cost is acceptable for transformations
invariants: Pipeline must be idempotent — re-running doesn't create duplicates
Errors must not silently drop data — use DLQ and monitoring
failure_modes: Watermark-based CDC misses late-arriving updates — use event time + watermark delay
Memory OOM in transform with unbounded data — use streaming with backpressure
Schema drift — new columns break downstream without schema evolution handling
counterarguments: For simple data migration, a single bulk load script may be more maintainable than a full ETL framework
evidence: Snowflake ELT best practices
Google Cloud ETL best practices
'Streaming Systems' by Akidau, Chernyak, Lax

entries.description: CI/CD, deployment, observability, and incident response patterns that remain stable across platform changes.

entries.title: CI/CD Pipeline Design and Deployment Strategies
entries.claim: CI/CD pipelines automate building, testing, and deployment; deployment strategies (blue-green, canary, rolling) control how new versions replace old ones, balancing speed, safety, and rollback capability.
entries.solution: CI (Continuous Integration): developers push to shared branch frequently; automated build + unit tests + linting run on every commit. CD (Continuous Delivery): every commit passes all tests → deployable artifact. CD (Continuous Deployment): every passing commit auto-deploys to prod. Stages: source → lint → build → unit test → integration test → security scan → deploy staging → smoke test → canary deploy → deploy prod. Deployment strategies: (1) Recreate — stop old, start new (downtime). (2) Rolling — replace instances gradually (slow rollback). (3) Blue-Green — two identical environments, switch traffic instantly (instant rollback, extra cost). (4) Canary — shift small traffic %, monitor metrics, gradually increase (slow but safe). (5) A/B testing — split by user segment. Feature flags decouple deploy from release. Health gates: pre-check (tests pass) + post-check (metrics within SLO).
assumptions: Automated tests provide sufficient quality signal
Deployment can be automated with rollback on health check failure
invariants: Every deployment must have a defined rollback path
Health checks must be faster than user timeout
failure_modes: Canary % too high — large blast radius if buggy
Health check passes but metrics degrade later — need SLO-based rollback
Feature flag not cleaned up — code complexity accumulates
counterarguments: For regulatory environments (finance, healthcare), manual approval gates may be required despite automation capability
evidence: Google SRE Workbook
Kubernetes deployment strategies documentation
AWS Well-Architected Framework

entries.title: Observability: Logs, Metrics, and Traces (The Three Pillars)
entries.claim: Observability rests on three pillars — logs (discrete timestamped events), metrics (numeric time-series measurements), and traces (request paths through distributed services) — which together enable understanding and debugging of system behavior.
entries.solution: Logs: structured (JSON) with trace_id, span_id, timestamp, severity, component. Aggregated via Fluentd/Loki/ELK. Metrics: counters (monotonically increasing), gauges (current value), histograms (buckets for distributions), summaries. Tools: Prometheus (pull), StatsD (push). RED metrics (per service): Rate, Errors, Duration. USE metrics (per host): Utilization, Saturation, Errors. Traces: distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry/Zipkin/Jaeger), spans with start/end/parent-child. Correlation: propagate trace_id across logs/metrics/traces via context propagation (W3C TraceContext). Alerting: 90th percentile latency, error rate > 1%, saturation > 80%. SLOs + error budget: if error budget consumed > 80%, freeze releases.
assumptions: Instruments are added at service boundaries and critical paths
Tracing context is propagated across service calls (HTTP headers)
invariants: Trace IDs must be consistent across all telemetry for a request
Logs without trace context are uncorrelated noise
failure_modes: Too many alerts — alert fatigue and ignored pages
High-cardinality labels (user_id, request_id) — Prometheus OOM
Missing instrumentation on new endpoints — blind spot in production
counterarguments: For monolithic applications, traces add complexity without proportional benefit — focus on metrics + logs
evidence: by Liz Fong-Jones, Ben Hartman, and Emily Nakashima
Google SRE Workbook on monitoring
OpenTelemetry documentation

entries.title: SRE: Error Budgets, Toil, and On-Call
entries.claim: Site Reliability Engineering balances reliability and feature velocity using error budgets (allowed unreliability), eliminates toil (manual operations work), and structures on-call for sustainable incident response.
entries.solution: Error budget: SLO (e.g., 99.9% latency < 200ms) → budget = 0.1% * total requests. If budget consumed, freeze features (focus on reliability). Burn rate alerts: 'burn budget at >14.4x rate for 5 min' (fast burn) or '>6x for 30 min' (slow burn). Toil: >50% manual, repetitive, automatable. Eliminate by automation (runbooks → playbooks → bots). On-call: primary + secondary. Primary receives pages; secondary assists. Alert routing: by service ownership. Post-incident: blameless postmortem (timeline, root cause, action items), track MTTR, publish writeups. Runbooks for common incident types (latency spike, database failover, circuit breaker stuck open).
assumptions: SLOs are derived from business SLAs and user impact
On-call responds within defined SLA (e.g., 5 min)
invariants: Error budgets reset each period (rolling window)
Toil reduction is a measurable goal — track % time spent on manual tasks
failure_modes: SLOs set too lenient — quality degrades unnoticed
Too many pages — on-call burnout and alert fatigue
Postmortems become blame exercises — reduces reporting and learning
counterarguments: For small teams (1-2 engineers), dedicated SRE role is impractical — dev team handles ops with automation focus
evidence: Google SRE Workbook and 'Site Reliability Engineering' book (Beyer, Jones, Petoff)
Microsoft's 'The Art of SRE'

entries.title: HTTPS/TLS: Certificates, Mutual TLS, and Certificate Management
entries.claim: HTTPS uses TLS (Transport Layer Security) to encrypt and authenticate HTTP communication; certificates are verified via Certificate Authority (CA) chains, with automated management via Let's Encrypt/ACME and mutual TLS for service-to-service authentication.
entries.solution: TLS handshake: (1) Client hello (supported cipher suites, TLS version). (2) Server hello (selected cipher + version). (3) Certificate exchange (server sends X.509 chain). (4) ServerKeyExchange (for ECDHE key exchange). (5) ServerHelloDone. (6) ClientKeyExchange + ChangeCipherSpec + Finished. (7) Server ChangeCipherSpec + Finished. Certificate: contains subject, issuer, validity, public key, signature. Verification: OCSP/CRL revocation check + chain to trusted root. Let's Encrypt: free CA using ACME protocol. certbot/lemur/automated renewal. mTLS: both client and server present certificates; used for service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) and API gateways. Certificate management: automate issuance + rotation (90-day certs), monitor expiry (Prometheus, CertSpotter). TLS 1.3: only 0-RTT or 1-RTT handshake, fewer ciphers, faster.
assumptions: Domain resolves to server with valid DNS records
Time is synchronized (cert validity checked against system clock)
invariants: Certificates expire — automated renewal is mandatory
Private key must never be committed to version control
failure_modes: Certificate expired — site unreachable for all users
Intermediate cert missing — browser warnings
mTLS client cert issued to wrong service — access denied silently
counterarguments: For internal-only services within a private network, TLS may add latency overhead — but is still recommended for defense in depth
evidence: Let's Encrypt ACME documentation
Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator

entries.description: Testing fundamentals, TDD, and quality assurance principles that remain stable across languages and frameworks.

entries.title: Testing Pyramid and Test Strategy
entries.claim: The testing pyramid prescribes a ratio of unit tests (many, fast) to integration tests (fewer, slower) to end-to-end tests (fewest, slowest), ensuring fast feedback and reliable coverage without excessive maintenance cost.
entries.solution: Pyramid (left to right): (1) Unit tests — test individual functions/classes/methods in isolation with mocks for dependencies. 70% of tests. Fast (<100ms), run on every commit. (2) Integration tests — test module/service interactions (DB, API, queue, external service contracts). 20%. Slower (seconds), detect integration bugs. (3) E2E/UI tests — test full user flows through the UI. 10%. Slowest, flaky, brittle. TDD: Red (write failing test) → Green (write minimal code to pass) → Refactor (improve design, tests still green). Properties: correctness of behavior, regression prevention, documentation (executable spec), design improvement (forces testable, small functions). Test quality: arrange-act-assert structure, independent (no shared state), fast, deterministic, isolated.
assumptions: Tests run in isolated environment (separate DB, mocks for external services)
Test suite can run in parallel for fast feedback
invariants: Unit tests should never touch network/database (mock them)
E2E tests should be tagged and run separately from unit tests
failure_modes: Inversion — too many E2E tests (slow CI) or too few unit tests (bugs slip through)
Brittle tests — depend on ordering, time, or shared mutable state
Testing implementation details instead of behavior — breaks on refactor
counterarguments: For some domains (UI-heavy apps), E2E tests are unavoidable — invest in visual regression and flaky test detection instead
evidence: Martin Fowler 'Test-Driven Development' (2005), 'Google Testing Blog'
A. K. Bently's 'Continuous Delivery'

entries.title: Property-Based Testing and Fuzz Testing
entries.claim: Property-based testing validates general properties of code (not specific examples) by generating random inputs, while fuzz testing provides malformed/random inputs to discover crashes, panics, and security vulnerabilities.
entries.solution: PBT: define properties (laws) that should always hold, then framework generates random test cases. Classic properties: (1) Round-trip — serialize then deserialize returns original. (2) Idempotency — f(f(x)) = f(x). (3) Commutativity/Associativity. (4) Invariants — postconditions always hold. (5) Metamorphic — related inputs give related outputs. Frameworks: Hypothesis (Python, generates from strategy), QuickCheck (Haskell), jqwik (Java), fast-check (TypeScript). Shrinking finds minimal failing case. Fuzz: provide malformed/edge inputs (empty, huge, null bytes, unicode edge cases) to find crashes, OOM, panics. Tools: AFL, libFuzzer, American Fuzzy Lop, Hypothesis fuzzy. Coverage: aim for edge cases — empty string, max int, boundary values, special chars.
assumptions: Property is correctly stated (false properties fail with valid inputs)
Test cases can be meaningfully randomized within constraints
invariants: Generated inputs should respect type/contract constraints
Shrinking must produce minimal, reproducible counterexample
failure_modes: Non-deterministic tests — generated input occasionally fails, hard to debug
Overfitting tests to specific generated cases rather than true properties
Property too weak — passes but doesn't catch real bugs
counterarguments: For domain-specific edge cases, hand-written example tests complement PBT better than relying solely on random generation
evidence: Hypothesis documentation
Fred Brooks 'No Silver Bullet' (on accidental vs essential complexity)
Google OSS-Fuzz continuous fuzzing project

entries.title: Chaos Engineering and Resilience Testing
