entries.claim: Chaos engineering validates system resilience by injecting realistic failures (process kills, network partitions, latency, disk full) into production-like environments to discover weaknesses before they cause real outages.
entries.solution: Principles: (1) Hypothesis — define normal behavior baseline. (2) Steady state — automated metric for system health. (3) Vary real world — simulate real incidents. (4) Run in prod — small blast radius, but real conditions. (5) Automate experiments — run continuously. (6) Minimize blast radius — start small. Experiment design: (1) Identify steady-state (requests/sec > X, latency < Y). (2) Form hypothesis — 'if we kill one replica, system should sustain'. (3) Design experiment — kill process via SIGTERM, inject network latency 500ms, fill disk. (4) Run and measure. Tools: Chaos Monkey (Netflix), Gremlin, Chaos Mesh (K8s). Common experiments: instance termination, network partition (2/3 replicas), CPU/memory hog, DNS failure, dependency service down. Game days — scheduled team exercises running chaos experiments.
assumptions: Steady-state metrics are reliable and automated
Recovery mechanisms (circuit breaker, retry, failover) are properly configured
invariants: Experiments must have a rollback plan and clear stop conditions
Small blast radius — single AZ, single service, low traffic %
failure_modes: Too much chaos too fast — cascading failure in prod
Not monitoring during experiment — miss the impact
Chaos without hypothesis — just breaking things without learning
counterarguments: For early-stage systems, tabletop exercises and staging chaos may provide sufficient value before prod chaos
evidence: Principles of Chaos Engineering (PrinciplesOfChaos.org)
Netflix Chaos Engineering whitepapers
Google SRE Workbook on load testing

entries.description: Web protocols, browser APIs, and frontend fundamentals that change slowly.

entries.title: HTTP API Security Best Practices
entries.claim: Securing HTTP APIs requires authentication (JWT/OAuth2), authorization (RBAC), rate limiting, input validation, TLS enforcement, CORS policies, and security headers to defend against common attacks.
entries.solution: Authentication: (1) Pass tokens via Authorization header (not URL — logged in server/proxy logs). (2) JWT with short expiry + refresh token rotation. (3) OAuth 2.1 with PKCE for public clients. Authorization: RBAC — check permission for every endpoint via middleware; deny by default. Rate limiting: token bucket or sliding-window counter per user/IP/key; return 429 + Retry-After. CORS: allowlist specific origins; no wildcard for creds-enabled. Credentials: only include with explicit origin allowlist. Security headers: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS), X-Content-Type-Options (nosniff), Content-Security-Policy (restrict scripts/objects), X-Frame-Options (DENY/SAMEORIGIN — clickjacking), Referrer-Policy (same-origin), Permissions-Policy. Input validation: schema validation (JSON schema/Zod), type checking, length limits, SQL injection prevention (parameterized queries). TLS: enforce HTTPS, redirect HTTP, use modern TLS 1.3, strong cipher suites. Body size limits to prevent DoS. Pagination with LIMIT/OFFSET or cursor (keyset) for large result sets.
assumptions: API is served over HTTPS in production
Authentication tokens are stored securely (HttpOnly Secure cookies preferred over localStorage)
invariants: Never trust client-side validation — always re-validate server-side
Apply rate limiting before heavy processing, return 429 early
failure_modes: JWT in URL — leaked via referrer/logs
CORS wildcard with credentials — any origin can make requests
No input size limits — attacker sends MB-sized payloads causing OOM
counterarguments: For public APIs with high traffic, a CDN/API gateway (Cloudflare, Kong) at edge provides rate limiting + WAF before reaching application
evidence: OWASP API Security Top 10
OWASP ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard)
RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7519 (JWT)

entries.title: Browser Rendering Pipeline and Performance Optimization
entries.claim: Browsers render pages through a pipeline (DOM → CSSOM → Render tree → Layout → Paint → Composite) that can be optimized by understanding reflow triggers, layer compositing, resource loading strategies, and memory lifecycle.
entries.solution: Rendering pipeline: (1) Parsing — HTML parser builds DOM (blocking), CSS parser builds CSSOM (non-blocking if async). (2) Render tree — DOM + CSSOM combined, computed styles. (3) Layout — compute geometry (reflow, expensive). (4) Paint — fill pixels (rasterize), layer by layer. (5) Composite — GPU layers combined. Reflow triggers: DOM mutations (add/remove element, change class, innerHTML), reading offsetWidth/clientHeight (forces synchronous layout — 'read-write' thrashing). Optimization: (1) Lazy loading (loading='lazy' for images/iframe) — defer off-viewport resources. (2) Code splitting — dynamic import(). (3) Critical CSS inline (above fold). (4) Async/defer scripts to not block parsing. (5) Image optimization (WebP/AVIF, responsive srcset, width descriptor). (6) Minimize reflows — batch DOM reads/writes. (7) use-transform-instead-of-changing-layout-properties (translateZ for GPU layer).
assumptions: Page loads primarily over HTTPS with HTTP/2+
Browser supports modern APIs (IntersectionObserver, native lazy loading)
invariants: Reduce DOM size — fewer than ~1500 elements and < 100ms layout time
Critical rendering path should deliver content (FCP/LCP) before heavy JS execution
failure_modes: Layout thrashing — reading then writing DOM in a loop causes repeated reflows
Heavy main-thread JS blocks rendering and user input
Images without dimensions — causes layout shift (CLS) affecting Core Web Vitals
counterarguments: For static marketing sites, static site generators (Next.js, Astro) with edge rendering may outperform client-side hydration
evidence: Web.dev performance guides
Google Chrome DevTools documentation
Web Core Vitals (LCP, FID, CLS)

entries.description: Foundational mathematics and logic for reasoning, probability, and computational correctness.

entries.title: Bayes' Theorem and Probabilistic Reasoning
entries.claim: Bayes' theorem describes how to update probability estimates (posteriors) given new evidence, relating prior belief, likelihood, and marginal probability in a precise mathematical framework.
entries.solution: P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B). Where P(A) is the prior (belief before evidence), P(B|A) is the likelihood (probability of evidence given hypothesis), P(B) is the marginal (total probability of evidence), and P(A|B) is the posterior (updated belief). Naive Bayes classifier applies Bayes with independence assumption between features. Applications: (1) Medical diagnosis — P(disease|symptom) from P(symptom|disease) and P(disease). (2) Spam filtering — P(spam|words) from training corpus. (3) A/B testing — posterior probability that one variant is better. (4) Bayesian updating — prior from previous experiment. Base rate neglect — always incorporate P(A) (prior probability), not just P(B|A).
assumptions: Events A and B have known P(B|A) and P(A)
P(B) > 0 so denominator is non-zero
invariants: P(A) + P(not A) = 1 (probabilities sum to 1)
More evidence should change the posterior — Bayesian updating is iterative
failure_modes: Base rate neglect — ignoring prior P(A), only using P(B|A) — common cognitive bias
Assuming independence (naive Bayes) when features are correlated — accuracy degrades
Using point estimates instead of distributions — loses uncertainty information
counterarguments: Bayesian methods require specifying priors which may be subjective — frequentist methods avoid priors but can't update with evidence in the same way
evidence: Jaynes 'Probability Theory: The Logic of Science'
McGraynor & Sobel 'Understanding Odds and Probability'

entries.title: Boolean Algebra and Logic Foundations
entries.claim: Boolean algebra over two values (true/false, 0/1) with operations AND, OR, NOT forms the mathematical foundation of digital circuits and computing, with identities (De Morgan's, idempotent, distributive) enabling circuit optimization.
entries.solution: Operations: A AND B (both true), A OR B (either true), NOT A (inverted), A XOR B (exactly one). Identities: (1) Identity: A AND 1 = A, A OR 0 = A. (2) Idempotent: A AND A = A, A OR A = A. (3) Complement: A AND NOT A = 0, A OR NOT A = 1. (4) Commutative: A AND B = B AND A. (5) Associative: (A AND B) AND C = A AND (B AND C). (6) Distributive: A AND (B OR C) = (A AND B) OR (A AND C). (7) De Morgan: NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B); NOT(A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B). Karnaugh maps (K-maps) — graphical method to minimize Boolean expressions for up to 4-6 variables. Truth tables enumerate all 2^n input combinations. Logic gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND (universal), NOR (universal), XOR, XNOR.
assumptions: Binary logic (no fuzzy/ternary values)
Operations are deterministic and noise-free
invariants: NAND and NOR gates are functionally complete — any Boolean function can be built from NAND alone
De Morgan's laws enable transformation between AND and OR representations
failure_modes: Incorrect operator precedence — NOT binds tighter than AND/OR, AND binds tighter than OR
XOR vs OR confusion — XOR is exclusive, OR is inclusive
Not simplifying expressions — extra gates in circuit, wasted hardware
counterarguments: For simple conditions, explicit Boolean expressions are more readable than minimized forms — optimize only in hardware or hot paths
evidence: Claude Shannon 'A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits' (1938)
Boolean algebra textbook standard

entries.title: Graph Theory: Basic Definitions and Algorithms
entries.claim: Graphs (vertices connected by edges) model pairwise relationships, with fundamental algorithms (shortest path, spanning tree, topological sort, strongly connected components) solving real-world problems from network routing to dependency resolution.
entries.solution: Definitions: Directed vs undirected, weighted vs unweighted, simple (no self-loops, no multi-edges), multigraph, complete graph, cycle, DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph). Representations: Adjacency list (O(V+E) space, best for sparse), adjacency matrix (O(V^2) space, good for dense/frequent edge checks). Algorithms: (1) Shortest path: Dijkstra (non-negative weights, O((V+E)log V)), Bellman-Ford (handles negative, detects negative cycle O(VE)), Floyd-Warshall (all-pairs O(V^3)). (2) MST: Kruskal (union-find, O(E log E)), Prim (O((V+E)log V)). (3) Topological sort (DFS-based, only for DAG — detects cycles). (4) SCC: Tarjan or Kosaraju's (find strongly connected components). (5) BFS/DFS. (6) Bipartiteness check (2-coloring via BFS). (7) Graph traversal: Eulerian path (all edges once), Hamiltonian path (all vertices once).
assumptions: Graph fits in memory (or use external sort for very large graphs)
Graph representation matches algorithm needs
invariants: Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights — use Johnson's for negative weights
Topological sort possible iff graph is a DAG
failure_modes: Dijkstra on negative weights — produces incorrect results
Not detecting cycles in topological sort attempt — infinite loop in recursive DFS
Wrong graph representation — adjacency matrix on sparse graph wastes memory
counterarguments: For streaming/graph database scenarios, online algorithms (reservoir sampling, HyperLogLog for cardinality) may be more appropriate
evidence: CLRS 'Introduction to Algorithms' — Graph chapters
Sedgewick & Wayne 'Algorithms' (4th ed) — Part II: Graph Algorithms

entries.description: General problem-solving, debugging, and decision methodologies applicable across all domains.

entries.title: First-Principles Thinking and Problem Decomposition
entries.claim: First-principles thinking decomposes complex problems into fundamental truths (assumptions that cannot be questioned) and builds solutions from those axioms, avoiding the constraints of reasoning by analogy.
entries.solution: Process: (1) Identify the problem clearly. (2) Break down into constituent parts/sub-problems (divide and conquer). (3) Identify assumptions — ask 'What do I actually know to be true?' Strip away inherited beliefs. (4) Question each assumption — is it provable, or just conventional wisdom? (5) Rebuild from fundamental truths using first principles. (6) Identify the real constraints (physics, math, economics, not 'how it's always been done'). (7) Design from the constraints. Example: Elon Musk on rocket cost — everyone assumed rockets are expensive because 'that's how much it costs'; first-principles: raw material cost is a small fraction; build from aluminum + oxygen + pressure vessels = reusable rocket. Tools: the 'Five Whys' technique to peel back layers of assumption.
assumptions: The problem can be broken into independent, solvable sub-problems
Fundamental truths are discoverable and unambiguous
invariants: More first-principles decomposition usually reveals cheaper/better solutions
Questioning authority/assumptions is necessary for breakthrough innovation
failure_modes: Over-decomposing — losing sight of practical constraints and market realities
Reinventing the wheel when existing solutions already embody first principles
Not knowing what counts as a 'fundamental truth' in the domain — domain expertise required
counterarguments: First-principles thinking is cognitively expensive and slow — sometimes reasoning by analogy (comparing to proven solutions) is the pragmatic choice under time pressure
evidence: Elon Musk's TED talk on first principles thinking
Darwin's 'Origin of Species' as first-principles biology
Feynman's approach to physics

entries.title: Root Cause Analysis: 5 Whys and Fishbone (Ishikawa) Diagram
entries.claim: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) systematically identifies the fundamental underlying cause of a problem rather than treating symptoms, using techniques like the 5 Whys (iterative questioning) and fishbone diagrams (categorizing contributing factors).
entries.solution: 5 Whys: Start with a problem statement, ask 'Why did this happen?' 5 times, each answer becomes the input to the next 'Why'. Stop when you reach a process/system root cause (not a person). Example: 'Car won't start' → 'Battery dead (why)' → 'Alternator not charging (why)' → 'Belt broken (why)' → 'Insufficient visual inspection (why)' → 'No maintenance checklist (why)' → 'Missing preventive maintenance process'. Fishbone (Ishikawa): categories on 'bones' — People, Methods, Machines, Materials, Measurements, Environment. Each team member adds contributing factors. Pareto analysis — 80/20: focus on vital few causes. Techniques: 'But why?' for depth, 'How can effect recurrence be prevented?' for solution design.
assumptions: The problem has a definable root cause rather than being systemic/random
Contributing factors can be identified through team collaboration and data analysis
invariants: Root cause should be process/system-level, not person-level
Solutions must address the root cause, not just symptoms
failure_modes: Stopping too early — treating symptoms instead of root cause
Blaming individuals instead of fixing processes — causes cover-ups
Asking 'why' too many times — loses connection to original problem
counterarguments: For intermittent/non-reproducible bugs, RCA by interview alone may miss the true cause — combine with data from logs and metrics
evidence: Toyota Production System (Taiichi Ohno on 5 Whys)
Kaplan & Norton on fishbone diagrams
NASA 5-step RCA (ESA reliability guide)

entries.title: Occam's Razor and the Principle of Least Assumption
entries.claim: Occam's Razor states that among competing hypotheses that make the same predictions, the one with the fewest assumptions (simplest explanation) should be selected, avoiding unnecessary complexity.
entries.solution: When diagnosing a problem, start with the simplest explanation that fits all facts, then add complexity only if simpler explanations are falsified. Practical application: (1) Check recent changes first — the new deploy is most likely. (2) Reproduce before investigating — confirm the problem pattern. (3) Eliminate variables systematically — change one thing at a time. (4) Check the obvious first (config, permissions, network, logs) before diving into complex theories. (5) Use the 'minimum viable hypothesis' — the smallest set of changes that could cause the observed symptom. Warning: 'simplest' doesn't mean 'oversimplified' — must still account for all evidence.
assumptions: Complex explanations can be decomposed into multiple interacting causes
Evidence constrains the hypothesis space
invariants: A good hypothesis explains ALL observations, not just the most striking one
Complexity should be added only when necessary to explain evidence
failure_modes: Over-simplifying — dismissing valid but complex explanations prematurely
Confirmation bias — finding the simplest explanation that confirms preconception, ignoring contradictory evidence
Assuming 'it was working before the change' when the root cause predated the change
counterarguments: Some phenomena (quantum mechanics, complex distributed systems) are inherently complex and resist simple explanations
evidence: William of Ockham (14th century), Newton's 'Hypotheses Non Fingo' ('I do not feign hypotheses')
Carl Sagan on 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence'

implementation_notes.retrieval_strategy: Embed each artifact's claim+solution text (768-dim), store with metadata {category_id, domain, type, confidence, verification_status, tags}. Query via search_semantic or search_learned_facts. RAGPipeline.retrieve_context with n=5 and threshold 0.15 for degraded mode.
implementation_notes.update_cadence: Evergreen entries (last_verified='static') need no routine review. Versioned entries (last_verified=ISO date) reviewed quarterly. Add new domains incrementally — each domain is a separate JSON array for selective loading.
implementation_notes.confidence_field_usage: confidence:0.95-1.0 (verified facts, mathematical laws) are always returned. 0.90-0.95 (well-established practices) returned with note. <0.90 entries suppressed in degraded mode unless no higher-confidence match found.
implementation_notes.fallback_chain: ChromaDB vector search -> SQLite TF-IDF keyword match -> MemoryVault (memory_vault.json) -> hardcoded generic response. Each layer independent of network.
implementation_notes.size_budget: Each artifact: text ≤ 700 chars, metadata ≤ 100 bytes. At ~800 bytes/record, 1500 records = ~1.2MB raw, ~600KB compressed embeddings (384 dim * 4 bytes = 1.5KB/vector). Fits easily in free-tier Render disk.
